extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, rulemaking practitioners, policymakers, prosecutors, and legislators concerned with public comment processes and mass/malattributed comments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for federal agencies (and related actors) on identifying, processing, and legally assessing mass, computer-generated, and malattributed public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking, including technological responses and potential criminal or APA implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of public reaction as evidence of controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the large number of comments and strong criticism can demonstrate that the effects of an action are controversial (e.g., Sierra Club v. Bosworth: 'Given the large number of comments, close to 39,000, and the strong criticism ... we cannot summarily conclude that the effects ... are not controversial').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have considered the sheer volume and intensity of comments as part of the 'controversial' inquiry under NEPA; large outpourings and substantial dispute as to size, nature, or effect can demonstrate controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of relying on coordinated/form letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may rely on letters even if numerous people 'share the same opinion and pooled their efforts'—such pooling does not necessarily undermine the intended show of support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Resident Councils of Wash. v. Leavitt) has upheld agency reliance on coordinated/form comments; agencies are not automatically barred from treating coordinated submissions as evidence of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content versus mere statements of preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Many mass comments are general statements of support or opposition rather than detailed, substantive input; there is debate over whether and to what extent agencies should consider comments that contain only statements of preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers find a large percentage of mass-response comments lack substantive content. Agencies must decide the weight to give pure preference statements versus data-driven or legal argumentation when finalizing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of comment volume and sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether agencies should take the number of comments and the sentiment expressed into account when finalizing a rule (the Permanent Subcommittee recommended Congress consider amending the APA to provide guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance from Congress could help agencies decide if and when to consider volume/sentiment; absent such guidance, agencies vary in practice and may reference counts opportunistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness and selection bias of commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments are a self-selected sample and generally do not reliably reflect broader public opinion; commenters may disproportionately be from relatively privileged groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should account for potential selection bias — the views in the comment record may not be representative and may overrepresent organized or advantaged interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting commenter influence: sophistication and source
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of sophistication in comments and the source (e.g., business vs. citizen) affect the likelihood agencies will alter proposals in response to comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies find business comments are often more meticulously drafted and more likely to influence agencies; agencies place high value on hard data and source credibility when weighing comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency approaches to opinions expressed in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Three distinct approaches: (a) opinions are irrelevant—only factual content matters; (b) opinions are relevant to political perception and may affect agency activities or rollout; (c) opinions are relevant insofar as they express popular sentiment and may be considered but never as the sole factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies vary in which approach they adopt; interview data show officials uniformly say the process is 'not a vote' but differ in how they factor expressed opinions into decisionmaking and implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of de-duplication (de-duping) software to process mass comments
rubrics_metrics.description: De-duping software scans comments, compares overlap, and groups comments that appear to derive from a common source to reduce processing burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duping can massively decrease processing time by batching identical or near-identical comments; it focuses on word content and order and may not detect synonym substitutions or paraphrasing; OCR quality limits electronic processing of paper submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting overlap thresholds for de-duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must set the threshold (e.g., 90% identity) at which a comment is flagged as likely part of a mass comment campaign; different agencies use different thresholds and none appears to require 100% overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threshold choice affects what is batched; lower thresholds will flag more altered duplicates but may risk grouping legitimately distinct comments. Agencies should adopt and document a consistent threshold policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of de-duplication (text-only comparison and evasion techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: De-duping software focuses on actual words and their order; it will not recognize duplication if submitters change words to synonyms or substantially rephrase content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should be aware that adversaries can evade detection by synonym substitution or rewording; manual review or other analytic techniques may be required for sophisticated evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unique or partially unique content within mass campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when identical content is batched, agencies generally review unique information added by submitters (e.g., a sentence on how the issue relates to them); partially unique comments are more challenging to process than identical ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duping can reduce marginal processing time for identical comments to near zero, but comments with unique additions may not be flagged and require substantive review; agencies should have procedures to surface and evaluate unique content within batched groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting and public display policies for mass-submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies do not post all iterations of comments on Regulations.gov if they qualify as part of a mass comment campaign; certain agencies post a representative example instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about what to post affect transparency and public access to the record; agencies should establish posting policies (e.g., representative sampling) and explain them in the record where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative burden and cost considerations from duplicate comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate or near-duplicate comments impose real processing costs on agencies without adding substantive content to the rulemaking record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duping and batching are justified in part by cost-savings; agencies should balance resource constraints with the need to capture unique substantive input and maintain a transparent record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding organizers' motivations for mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizers run mass comment campaigns for varied goals including calling attention to a rulemaking, increasing membership and contributions, and moving members up the 'ladder of engagement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizing diverse motivations helps agencies contextualize campaigns and distinguish between advocacy goals versus attempts to distort the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that the notice-and-comment process is not a vote
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies uniformly assert that notice-and-comment is not a vote—agencies do not simply tabulate 'pro' and 'anti' comments and adopt the more popular position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle should guide how agencies use counts and sentiment: while political perceptions may matter, substantive legal and factual analysis remains primary in decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive concerns posed by malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments involve a direct falsehood about identity and may harm individuals whose names are used; they raise particular legal and policy issues distinct from mass or computer-generated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattribution may be characterized as identity theft by some observers; agencies should consider both harms to the integrity of the rulemaking process and harms to third parties whose identities are misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of potential criminal liability for malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Various criminal provisions might conceivably apply to malattributed comments—fraud, making false statements, computer crime, identity theft, mail/wire fraud, conspiracy statutes—but applicability is uncertain and fact-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and prosecutors should examine statutes (e.g., 18 U.S.C. §§ 1341, 1343, 1037, 1030, 371, 1001, 1028) and relevant elements; absent clear precedent, referrals to DOJ may be appropriate in significant cases, recognizing prosecutorial discretion and evidentiary hurdles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and limits of common-law fraud to malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraud requires five elements: (1) false statement of material fact, (2) knowledge the statement is untrue, (3) intent to deceive, (4) justifiable reliance by the victim, and (5) injury to the victim; malattributed comments may meet some elements but often fail on reliance, materiality, or demonstrable injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies typically do not 'rely on' commenter identity, showing justifiable reliance and injury may be difficult. Fraud statutes requiring money or property loss are typically ill-suited for influence-seeking submissions to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential reach (and limits) of conspiracy-to-defraud statute (18 U.S.C. §371)
rubrics_metrics.description: §371 has been read broadly to reach conspiracies to impair, obstruct, or defeat lawful government functions; submitting false identities to create the appearance of support could, in theory, be framed as an attempt to impair agency functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application here is uncertain and differs from traditional 'Klein conspiracies'; proving conspiracy and sufficient harm may be difficult and prosecutors may be disinclined absent clear obstruction or significant impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of false-statements statute (18 U.S.C. §1001) and materiality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: §1001 prohibits 'false, fictitious, or fraudulent' statements to a federal agency; a key issue is materiality—a false statement must have a natural tendency to influence, or be capable of influencing, the decision of the decisionmaking body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A false name may be immaterial where agencies focus only on substantive content; however, bespoke misstatements that claim unique, relevant expertise or background could be material (e.g., falsely asserting to be a Ph.D. chemist or a long-term employee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligations to refer suspected criminal activity to DOJ
rubrics_metrics.description: If malattributed comment activity constitutes a crime, an important federal response would be prosecution and agencies may be expected to refer significant examples to the Department of Justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports note that agencies rarely made such referrals historically; agencies should consider protocols for referral where evidence suggests criminality and document their decisions.
